opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest difference is the feedback loop, and what that does to how you think.

When you build an experimental apparatus, every iteration is expensive. You order parts, you wait, you align things, something leaks or drifts, and maybe after weeks you get one data point you trust. So you're forced to think very carefully before you act. You do a lot of reasoning on paper first, because being wrong costs you a month. There's a kind of craftsmanship to it. You develop intuition through your hands, and a lot of knowledge lives in the lab and in people's heads rather than in papers.

With numerical experiments, and especially with model training, the loop is much faster, at least at small scale. You can try an idea in the afternoon and see a curve by the evening. That changes your psychology. You become more empirical and more willing to just try things, because trying is often cheaper than thinking it through. Sometimes that's a strength. Sometimes it's a trap, because you can run many experiments without really understanding anything.

The interesting thing about large model training is that it brings some of that experimental-physics flavor back. At the frontier scale, a run is costly, you can't repeat it many times, and there are a lot of messy engineering details, like numerics, infrastructure, and data, that behave like the "apparatus." You start caring about whether your instrument is calibrated. Is this loss spike real, or is it a bug? Is this improvement a real effect, or is it noise from the evaluation? That's very much the experimentalist's mindset: before you believe the signal, you have to believe your machine.

So I'd say small-scale numerical work feels like a theorist with a very fast calculator, and large-scale training feels surprisingly like running a big experiment. You need both instincts: be fast and exploratory where it's cheap, and be careful and skeptical where it's expensive.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts the cost and pace of numerical work with apparatus building, but does not say that Shunyu understands why procedures are necessary for numerical experiments while feeling at a loss when building apparatus.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest difference is where the uncertainty lives, and how fast it comes back to you.

When I was doing numerical experiments in physics, or now when I'm training models, the loop is very tight. You write code, you run it, and in a few minutes or a few hours you get a number back. If it's wrong, it's almost always your own mistake somewhere in the code or the setup, and you can go find it. The world you're interacting with is deterministic in principle. It's a world you built, so in a sense you already know all the rules, you're just discovering the consequences. That's actually very satisfying, because the feedback is clean and you can iterate dozens of times a day. Your intuition develops quickly because you get so many samples.

Building apparatus is completely different. I only did a bit of experimental work, but it was enough to feel it. The loop is slow, sometimes weeks, and when something doesn't work, the space of reasons is enormous and most of them are not intellectual. A cable is loose. There's a ground loop. The temperature in the room drifted. Someone bumped the optical table. Nature doesn't care about your model, and it also doesn't tell you which assumption you violated. You're debugging reality instead of debugging your own thinking, and reality has a much larger bug surface.

So the skills feel different too. Numerics rewards a certain kind of cleverness and speed, and also honesty with yourself, because it's very easy to fool yourself with a simulation that confirms what you wanted. Experiments reward patience and a kind of humility. You learn to respect that the system is bigger than you. I actually think that's a healthy thing to have experienced, because in machine learning we often slip into treating the model like a clean numerical object, when really once it's large enough it behaves more like an experimental system. You don't fully know why it does what it does, you have to form hypotheses, run careful controlled comparisons, worry about confounders. The GPU cluster even has its own version of the loose cable, like a bad node or a nondeterministic kernel.

What I would say is that training large models sits somewhere in between. The turnaround is faster than a physics experiment but slower than a classic simulation, and the object you're studying is partly designed and partly emergent. So the mindset I try to keep is from both sides. Move quickly and iterate like a numericist, but treat the results with an experimentalist's suspicion.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts fast, understandable numerical/model-training loops with slow apparatus debugging and many possible causes. It does not say that Yao is at a loss about why apparatus-building procedures are necessary.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest difference is how much control you have over the experiment. In a numerical experiment, you can often hold the setup fixed, change one variable, and run it again. The feedback loop is relatively fast. With physical apparatus, getting to the point where you can run a meaningful experiment is itself a large part of the work. If the result is unexpected, you have to ask whether your hypothesis is wrong or whether some part of the apparatus isn’t working as intended.

But AI model training sits somewhere in between. It happens in software, yet that doesn’t mean you fully understand or control it. You have the data, the optimization process, the implementation, and the evaluation all interacting. A failed run can be surprisingly difficult to interpret.

So the distinction, to me, is less about numerical versus physical experiments and more about how reliable your experimental system is. When the system is well established, you can focus on testing ideas. When it isn’t, building something that gives trustworthy feedback becomes the central scientific task.

r001.rationale: The candidate compares experimental control and feedback reliability, but does not say that Shunyu understands why procedures are necessary for numerical experiments or AI training while feeling at a loss about building apparatus.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the biggest difference is how much control you have over the environment. In a numerical experiment, you’ve already abstracted the world into code. If something goes wrong, you can often isolate a variable, rerun the experiment, and compare the results. Of course, model training still has randomness, and understanding why a model behaves a certain way can be very difficult.

When you build experimental apparatus, the abstraction itself is something you have to earn. You might think you’re testing one hypothesis, but the result also depends on whether the equipment is calibrated, whether a component is working, or whether there’s some effect you haven’t accounted for. A failed experiment could mean your idea is wrong, or simply that the apparatus isn’t doing what you think it’s doing.

So the feedback feels different. With code, you can iterate quickly, which makes it tempting to run more experiments. With physical apparatus, you have to spend more time making each experiment interpretable. I think that discipline is useful in AI too: before asking what a result tells us about intelligence, we should ask what we actually measured.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts control and iteration in numerical experiments with the calibration and interpretability challenges of physical apparatus, but it does not say that Yao understands why procedures are necessary in the former and is at a loss about building apparatus.
